subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED

speechtext: Hon. P. J. VENIOT (Postmaster General) moved the third reading of Bill No. 252, respecting certain employees of the postal or railway mail service of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
The bill which is now before
the house for its third reading is somewhat different in terms from the bill founded on the resolution which was first submitted for consideration by the Postmaster General. It offends a principle which we think should govern legislation of any character having to do with public servants who are reemployed in the service of the country after they have been dismissed from that service for good cause, or have left the service. This bill retroactively grants, in its terms, increases in pay to certain men on the basis of the employment which it is alleged they undertook when they reentered the service. I asked the Postmaster General to give the house some particulars with respect to the matter. It 
will be recalled that in 1919 this strike occurred. It will be further recalled that during the summer of 1919 tlhe employees in question were dismissed from the service because they declined to avail themselves of the opportunites which were offered by the administration for reemployment. Having thus left the service by reason of failing to obey a lawful command of the state to go back to their work, they were dismissed by order in council. It was later thought that, having regard to all the circumstances, these men should be afforded an opportunity to be reemployed in the public service, and to that end the difficulty was waived with respect to their age and they were permitted to apply for reemployment through the Civil Service Commission; and having been reemployed they reentered the service as new employees. Their salary was fixed; the compensation they were to receive was a matter of contract between them and the state. That compensation was not as much as the compensation they enjoyed before they left the service and this measure seeks, whether successfully or not, to provide that these men shall now receive pay on another basis than that of the contract which they made with the state when they were reemployed. We cannot get away from that fact. The question is whether or not this house will give effect to that principle, and in order that it may realize just what is involved I am going to give some illustrations from the documents brought down by the Postmaster General in order to clear away any misunderstanding. For instance, a large number of these men did not go to work for five or six years after they had been dismissed; a large number did not seek reemployment, some until after six years, many until after five years, some after four and others after three years, while others did not reenter the service until nine years after they were dismissed from their positions.
Now I will give a few illustrations, without using the names. Here is a man who was first employed on March 16, 1908; at the time of the strike he had been eleven years in the postal service. He was not reemployed until November 2, 1925, six years after he had been dismissed. At the time of his reemployment the bonus had disappeared from the public service and he received an initial salary of $1,020. At the time of his dismissal he was in receipt of a salary of $1,419, but by meritorious service in May of this year he reached a salary of $1,440, or $21 more than the salary he was receiving when he was

Western Postal Employees-Mr. Bennett
dismissed from his employment. It is now suggested by the Postmaster General that this man who, when he was dismissed from the service, was employed as a letter carrier, and who was later employed as a mail porter, should receive compensation on the basis of the salary and bonus he was receiving when he was dismissed from the service. This is the fifth case on the list.

is not alleged in that sense by those who are affected by this measure, and the reason I took this illustration was that the matter might be made perfectly clear before the bill is read the third time. Under the schedule provided by the Postmaster General it is stated that at the time this employee left the service through dismissal he was engaged as a letter carrier, and when he was later reemployed he went back as a mail porter. Now he is receiving SI,440, although at the time he left the service he was receiving $1,419, of which $480 was a bonus. When this man rejoined the service in 1925 he received a salary of $1,020, and the contention made outside of this house by those affected is that this employee is to receive his salary on the basis of the difference between what he was receiving at the time he was dismissed-

speechtext: No.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
I say that is the contention made outside this house by those affected; they contend that this man is to receive the difference between the amount he was receiving when he was dismissed and the amount he has received since going back to work.
Let me take another case which illustrates this wrong principle perhaps a little more Clearly. This employee first joined the service in 1914; he had worked in the department five years when he was dismissed, and he did not go back to work until six years after the strike. When he was dismissed he was receiving, with bonus, a salary of $1,419, but on May 1 of this year his salary was 78594-164J
$1,500. On both occasions he was employed as a letter carrier. Now, mark you, six years after he left the service he went back to work as a letter carrier, and when he was reemployed he received a salary of $1,200 although with the bonus, as I have said, he received $1,419 when he was dismissed. The contention is now made that he should receive additional compensation, although he was out of the service for six years before he went back to work as a letter carrier. The suggestion now is that he is to receive a salary not according to his employment but on the basis of what he would have received if he had not lost his job.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: That is not in the bill.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is what they are
contending it means, and the Postmaster General will say that that is their contention.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: Who are contending that?

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
The letter carrier in
this case.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: No.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
That man was a letter
carrier when he was dismissed and he is a letter carrier now; his case is number six on the schedule. As I pointed out, six years after he was dismissed he went back to work under a new contract with the state, and the salary he received was $1,200 although when he left six years previously he had been receiving a salary of $1,419. Now, by meritorious service, his salary has increased to $1,500, and my submission is that no body of men in the world can determine how much of the recommendation for meritorious service was attributable to his antecedent knowledge of the business and how much to the improvement which he showed from the time he was reemployed up to May 1, 1929. Remember that this man is now receiving almost $100 more than he was getting when he left the service; he has been at work now only three years, after having been out of the service of the government for six years, and now the Dominion of Canada is proposing to give him additional money. I submit that that is wrong.
Now let us take another case in order that there may be no misapprehension. The next case is a little stronger still; it is the second last case on the first page of the list. This employee first entered the service in 1909, and therefore had ten years of service when he was dismissed; I find that he was not reemployed until March 22, 1928, nine years after his employment with the state was seT
2578	COMMONS
Western Postal Employees-Mr. Bennett
ered. When he went back to work he was paid a salary of $1,020; when he left the employ of the state, according to the report furnished me, he received a salary of $1,300 and a bonus of $430, making a total of $1,730. On May 1, 1929, he was receiving only $1,140; he is now working as a postal helper, and when he left the service he was engaged as a primary sorter. He has been in the service now just over one year; he returned to work on March 22, 1928, and this is May 17, 1929. As I have said, he was reemployed at a salary of $1,020 and is now receiving $1,140, or $120 more than when he was reemployed some fifteen months ago. It is now asserted that he shall be paid on the basis of what he would have received as a postal helper had he continued his services without a break from the time he was first employed.
Let us go to the next case, the last one on the first sheet-I am not mentioning the names purposely. This man was reemployed in 1920, a year after the strike, at a salary and bonus amounting to $1,200. When he was dismissed from the service he was receiving $1,419. In both instances he had been working as a primary sorter. Look at what we are doing? That man made a definite contract with the state to work as a primary sorter a year after he was dismissed, the contract carrying a salary of $1,200 including bonus. When he left the year before he was receiving $1,419 and it is now contended that because he was employed as a primary sorter when he was dismissed and is employed as a primary sorter now that he shall be paid and compensated on the basis of $1,419 per year from the date of reemployment, although his contract calls for $1,200. In other words, the Dominion of Canada is to pay a man who makes a new contract, after he has struck in the public service and has been dismissed, $219 because he struck. That is the story.
Then we go to a case, which is found on the second page. This is a very striking case of a man who was employed in 1916, three years before the strike. He was dismissed after three years of service and did not go back to work until 1927, eight years after the strike. When he was reemployed he received $1,020; when he left the service he was receiving only $ 1,080 or $60 more than he received after being out of the service for eight years. He is now employed at a salary of $1,200 as a mail porter, and when he left the sendee he was employed as a letter carrier.
The next case is that of a man who was employed in 1918, about a year and a few
iMr. Bennett.]
months before he went on strike. He stayed out of the service four years, having come back on June 7, 1923. When he was reemployed he received $1,155 with bonus; when he was dismissed he was receiving $1,080. I want to show how this case works out. When he went back to work he received a larger sum of money than he was receiving when he left the service. He was receiving $1,620 on May 1st of this year, and in both instances he was employed as a subsorter.

speechtext: What page is that?

The second page, the

When reemployed he received $1,155 with the bonus; when he was dismissed his salary and bonus amounted to $1,080, and he is now receiving $1,620. He was employed as a subsorter at the time he left the service and was reemployed in that position. I put this to the house: How can you say that this man should have any adjustment of pay when he has been able so to conduct himself as to merit the appreciation of his employers to the extent of having his salary raised to $1,620?

He would not receive any
readjustment.

This man was taken back
after the strike as a subsorter, while the other case mentioned by the hon. leader of the opposition was that of a man who was taken back into a lower position but who did the work of a higher position; there is a difference between the two cases.

speechtext:
And these figures are
given by the Postmaster General. I go to the next case, that of a man who was engaged as a subsorter and who was acting in the same capacity when he was dismissed. This man had been a little more than a year in the service and he went back to work in November, 1920, a year after the strike. At the time he was reemployed he received $1,260 with the bonus, but when he was dismissed he was receiving only $1,080. He is now receiving $1,800 and is still working as a subsorter.

Western Postal Employees-Mr. Bennett

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: He has reached the maximum of his class.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Quite so, and he has
done that through meritorious service. I put this to the house:	Is it a sound principle
to say that you are going to differentiate between* the periods when meritorious service was rendered and go back to an antecedent period of time when a man received a certain amount of pay to determine what he is to receive in the light of what he should have received if he had not been so employed? That must be wrong, and the illustrations I have given prove it. That man would receive nothing under the readjustment; he would not even be considered according to the statement made by the Postmaster General.
The next case is that of a man first employed on March 18, 1912, seven years before the strike. He went back to work immediately after the strike, on November 10, 1919. He was reemployed at $1,202.50 including the bonus, but was receiving $1,206 when he was dismissed, and he is now receiving $1,740. When he was dismissed from the service he was employed as a raibsorter and when he went back to work he was taken on as a mail transfer agent. In other words, he went back to work as a mail transfer agent at $4 per year less than he was receiving when he was dismissed. It is suggested that he is to be paid as a substorter from the time he started to work. I would like the right hon. the Prime Minister to make the matter clear, because the statement of the employees as to what they are to receive is entirely at variance with what has been stated in the house, and I am taking this opportunity to illustrate the inequalities in order that a concise statement may be made with respect to what is to be done. Only this morning I was asked about it, and certainly the construction placed upon this matter is entirely different from that which the right hon. the Prime Minister and the Postmaster General suggested is the correct construction of the document.
The third case, on the top of page 3, is a very striking one. This employee had only been at work for a little over two months, having started to work on May 7, 1919, and having struck in July, 1919. He was reemployed six years after, on April 28, 1925, at a salary of $1,020; when he was dismissed his salary was $1,080, because there had been readjustments of salary during that time. He is now receiving a salary of $1,200 per annum. At the time he struck the position was purely temporary because he had not been long enough employed to be on the permanent
staff. The record shows that he went to work as a mail porter in 1925. What adjustment is possible in that case?
Let me pass to another case which illustrates the same principle. This employee went to work on the 2nd January, 1917, or a little more than two years before the strike. He went back to work on the first October, 1923, or about four years after the strike. When he went out on strike and was dismissed, his total salary and bonus amounted to $1,184.25. When he was reemployed his salary was $1,095 and it now amounts to $1,320. In both cases he was employed as a letter carrier. That is what this sheet shows. That is, he was employed as a letter carrier, as hon members will observe, four years after he was dismissed, and he is now receiving $1,320, on account of meritorious service based upon his ability as, I take it. At the time of his dismissal he was drawing $1,184.25, but when he went back to work he got only $1,095, and we are told there is to be a readjustment of that man's pay. This is plainly a case in which the Postmaster General says there is to be a readjustment. Can the country put itself behind such a principle? I leave it at that.
The next case i3 a very striking one, because this man was employed in June, 1914, five years before the strike, and he went back to work six years after the strike, namely, in 1925. The salary rate when he was reemployed was $1,020, there being no bonus. He has now risen to a salary of $1,500. At the time he left the service he was receiving $1,380. When he left the service he was enjoying the rank of a primary sorter; when he went back to work he got a position as a subsorter. In his case, according to the statements made-in the house, there is to be a readjustment, I cannot tell on what basis.
I come now to the last case that I will mention, because it is not necessary to take up further time. On the 1st May, 1917, this employee entered the public service of Canada. Two years and a few months later he was dismissed. He stayed out of the public service for three years. When he was reemployed he received $1,095, including bonus. When he was dismissed he was receiving $1,184.25. He has now risen to a salary of $1,500 and in both cases before and after the strike he is classified as a letter carrier. Can you readjust his pay? If so, on what principle?
I will not take up further time in dealing with these cases. I took them just at random as I looked over the pages, some of them indicating men who went back to work shortly

after the strike, and some who did not go bacll to work for some years after the strike, one indeed, for as long as seven years afterwards The contention is made that by reason oi particular experience in certain work men were able to render greater service to thft state than they otherwise would have been-, in other words, they were found to be better employees of the Post Office Department than they otherwise would have been. I am going to read to the house a letter I received from one of the officials of the Amalgamated Civil Servants who was himself employed in the post office at Winnipeg and who gives this illustration to me for the purpose of showing that although a man might nave been out of the service for a very considerable time, nevertheless his past experience was of importance. I use it to show just what the meaning of this proposal is. These are the exact words.
I joined tne public service of Canada on the 4th of November, 1919.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: What letter is this!

speechtext:
It is a letter written to
me by one of the members of the Amalgamated Civil Service.

speechtext: Will my hon. friend give his name?

.'Mr. MACKENZIE KING:	It is hardly
fair to read the letter if the hon. member does not give the name.

speechtext:
I am not bound to disclose the name of the correspondent. I do not fancy he has any objection to my giving it, but I am not doing so at the moment. He
;goes on :
I had postal experience in England, terminating ill 1911, when I came to Canada. As is usual with a young healthy immigrant, 1 turned my. hand to anything, and worked at all sorts of civilian duties absolutely unconnected with post office work. I enlisted in 1914, stayed with it until 1919, so I had ample time ill which to "forget".
The day after I entered the Winnipeg post office-
And hon. members will recollect that that was November 4, 1919.

I took over walk 36, head office-as a letter carrier, and surprised my officer, Mr. R. F. Ross, by having my walk routed up without assistance for the second delivery. I did that route for two weeks without assistance, even on the Monday, when all walks are heavy.

As a reward, another man was taken off walk 33, head office, and 1 was given me walk for my own. From the date I took that walk, early in December 1919 until Christmas 1919 1 trained three newcomers to the service, on walk 33 to see it they could do it, in order to give the supervisor the chance to use me as a "relief" man.
It was impossible to train a new man in so short a time, especially just before Christmas, so 1 retained the walk and now have a very good record as a carrier.
He is still a carrier.
I think my point is well taken and amply illustrated-that experience tells.
Let us see what we are doing. This young man receives his experience in England, not in Winnipeg. He did not strike sympathetically or otherwise. He joined the service of the state under a contract but because of his past experience that enabled him to do his work better than others, he was able to train others and his ambition being as it was, he found large." scope and wider opportunities because he desired to make progress. He now says that he has made that progress. The experience which he had in England was of assistance to Km as a letter carrier. Had he struck, had be been reemployed1, he would now comb back and get some pay from the country because it was said that he had experience in Canada before he struck. But being a man whose experience was derived in another country and who is not making it the basis of a claim for more pay, we are now told that he has no part or parcel in this transaction. He does not claim it, 1 may say. He is supporting the claim of these men.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: He supports their contention?

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
He is supporting his
fellow workers; he is their representative and the minister evidently has the letter in front of him also, so there is no question he knows to whom I refer. Having regard to the fact that men antecedently to employment may have been employed in a particular walk of life which enables them to do better the work in which they are engaged, and having regard to the fact that their employer must every year make recommendations as to their meritorious service, which recommendations, as I have pointed out, have resulted in many of these men receiving higher pay now than they had when they left the service, and in some cases receiving their maximum, is it not an unsound principle to say that because of the circumstances under which they left the service, you are to go back to their antecedent employment in order to determine the compensation they will receive.

Western Postal Employees-Mr. Bennett
If that principle can be applied as this gentleman thinks it can-and he is speaking for the Amalgamated Civil Servants of the country- as the Postmaster General and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) say the bill means, and as the Prime Minister says it does not, we can only look at the terms of the bill itself and ask ourselves what it does mean. What does the bill say? It says that these employees who subsequently were reemployed and are now in the said postal or railway mail service shall be paid for services actually performed as from the date of their reemployment at the rates of remuneration paid to other employees for similar services. That is a letter carrier is to be paid a letter carrier's pay.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: If he performs the work.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Yes, that is what I am
saying. A letter carrier is to be paid a letter carrier's pay. That is what he was before, and you cannot segregate the work that he did from the time of his reemployment against the experience that he has had in all these years and say that when he is promoted and receives additional pay it is referable only to the time of reemployment. It is referable to the whole experience he has had in life. It is so with everyone of us. I may have had experience in one particular line of work, and then have gone out of it, and come back to it. It is likely that the work will come back to me a little more readily because of my previous experience, and I am pushed up a little more quickly and reach the maximum of my class a little more rapidly than the other man. But we are now to say, that notwithstanding it was the experience that some one had somewhere else that enabled him to rise to the position he has reached without any assistance, he is not to share in any division of this money, although he has done this work, joining as a novice. Although he has had experience, he joins as a new employee, and he has now risen to the position where he is ranked as one of the very best of the employees, and yet he does not have anything to do with respect-to this $100,000 that is to be distributed. That is the sum which the Postmaster General says is to be distributed, and on the letters that are now before us as to the position of these gentlemen, I am satisfied that with the bill construed as it would be construed by a court, it would be very difficult to see how any employee would get anything. I am only pointing out to the house what the men think they are getting and what the bill itself says, and I leave it at that.
I cannot for my part bring myself to believe that it is a sound principle in a country like this to declare that because men received certain compensation before they sympathetically struck and left their employment, thereby tying up the public service, when they were reemployed and made a new contract with the state, and were reemployed because the state realized that the conditions were such that if possible they should use these men's services-I cannot believe that it is a sound principle not to punish them for striking. The only punishment according to this list that may be said to have been given to many of these men- the loss of seniority, whatever that may mean, they say is lost, because you cannot change the clock, time does not stand still. All that they have lost if this bill becomes operative is their seniority. The effect of it will be that some of them-not all, but some of them- are already saying that they have vindicated their position and that the postmaster at Winnipeg is to go. That is the next thing. They say:	We have got the government to
do this and now we are going to drive the postmaster out; we have got it started now. Thereby they are saying to the world that in the great struggle for the supremacy of law and order in this country against the forces of revolution and rebellion, this parliament is going to put the imprimatur of its approval upon the latter and not upon the former. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan) who is behind this move may think that it will bring great kudos to him from organized labour, but if my memory serves me well, in the long run it is the great labour forces in this country who are best served by the maintenance of law and order, and they look in the end to fair and even justice for the preservation of their rights, justice and fair play and fair treatment under every consideration. I am not unmindful of the effort that has been made in some quarters to induce me, for instance, to realize that those who supported this bill will be approved and those who did not will not be. I will not give my assistance to the forces of anarchy and the forces that brought disruption to the postal service of Canada, and I tell that to the Minister of Labour of this country. I tell him that he is doing no service to his own organizations when he does this, for the Postmaster General is but the medium through which the Minister of Labour expresses his opinion with respect to these matters.
I had hoped, very greatly hoped, that the retroactive features of this measure would be discarded, that we would not endeavour to adjust these matters as we are doing, but
*582	COMMONS
Western Postal Employees-Mr. Bennett
apparently the government thinks otherwise. The government thinks that it is going to bring some measure of peace and harmony out of discord and trouble by saying: We now recognize the principle that those who without notice left the service of the state, depriving the public of their opportunity for getting their mail, who disrupted a great public service, and who did that under circumstances to which we shall not now refer, should be rewarded and compensated for what they then did. If that be so, a precedent has been established which will have a far-reaching effect, and when you cloak it behind the hollow pretence of saying that men are going to be compensated for the work they do, that is cant and hypocrisy so far as the public is concerned, because every man who is employed to do a job and is seeking with ambition to advance his future and make a better place for himself in the world does not watch the clock and see how little he can do, but does the best that is in him by reason of the experience that he has had. Just as this man coming to this country in 1911 and working at various times after the war finally -went into the postal service in 1919 and was able in the light of his past knowledge to rise more rapidly and be of greater use to the public service and get in the end a higher classification and more pay than the man who joined the service as a novice, so these men in the light of the knowledge which they had knew when they reentered the service what they were doing; they made their contract with the state, and the state now says that it was not a contract such as they should have made, and the state is now going to make a new contract for them. I can only say that that principle I oppose. This bill is undoubtedly a modification of the first proposals. What it means I think it is difficult to say. It is not clearly stated. It is to be left to certain gentlemen to work out in the future, but when it is said that it involves 8100,000, it can only do that if the principles which the Postmaster General and the Minister of Labour have from time to time told these men would be applied, are applied.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
leader of the opposition is, I think, quite right in endeavouring to see that before this bill passes its third reading there should be left no possibility of misunderstanding as to what it means not only to hon. members in this house, but to those who may feel themselves entitled to some consideration under its provisions. With respect to his desire to have the meaning of the bill made perfectly clear, I have no exception to take. I would take very strong exception, however, to my hon. friend seeking to misrepresent in any way either the motive or the purpose of the Postmaster General or the Minister of Labour in so far as their association with the measure is concerned.
I will give to the house what the government understands to be the full force, meaning and effect of this bill, and if in any particular I am expressing a view which is other than that entertained by the Postmaster General or by the Minister of Labour, each of whom is in his seat at the moment, I hope he will correct me at once, because so far as the government is concerned there is no doubt in our minds as to what this measure contemplates, and there is one opinion only entertained by the cabinet with respect to its intention.
In a word, the bill means exactly what it says. I will read the section, omitting the few words that refer to certain orders in council. It is that:
the former employees of the postal or railway mail service of Canada who were removed from such service-
Then I skip a few words.
-and who were subsequently reemployed and are now in the said postal or railway mail service, shall be paid for services actually performed as from the date of their reemployment at the rates of remuneration paid to other employees for similar services.
That language is, I think, as plain as the English language can be. I do not believe it is possible to express in words a meaning more clearly than that expressed in this clause which in fact as the whole bill. It says that the employees are to be paid for services actually performed. My hon. friend has taken a table of statistics which has been supplied by the Postmaster General, and has placed his own interpretation upon their meaning. My hon. friend must have meant what he said as to the statistics leading to certain deductions which in fact he drew, but I am bound to say that so far as I can see no deductions of any kind whatever appear on the statement which is before my hon. friend
25S4	COMMONS
Western Postal Employees-Mr. Mackenzie King
What is recorded throughout is a mere statement of fact. There are no deductions or conditions set forth. I may be allowed to read the headings of the various matters referred to in the table:
Name of employee; jrear of birth; date of first employment; date of reemployment; salary rate when reemployed; salary bonus and total; salary rate when dismissed; salary bonus and total; salary May 1929; occupation at time of strike; occupation when reemployed.
These are the headings that appear on the table, and 'beneath them are given the facts or statistics that appropriately relate to the several headings. There are no deductions. My hon. friend has drawn his own inferences, and I confess that its seems to me he must have had in mind as he was doing so the resolution as it originally appeared on the order paper and his own interpretation thereof.

speechtext: May I ask my right hon. friend a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED

He will observe on page

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
I will answer
my hon. friend in a statement which will be applicable to all cases. Perhaps I may sim-plfy the matter by saying that insofar as this bill is concerned no account need be taken of the salary a man was receiving when he went out, no account need be taken of the date of his reemployment, no account need be taken of anything other than the actual work at which he has been engaged since his reemployment.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: I am very greatly obliged to the right hon. gentleman. That clarifies it very much.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
That is the
whole position. Now, may I go a step further? With respect to the salary that he receives when he is reemployed, as hon. gentlemen know, the Civil Service Commission attaches a certain rate of remuneration to each of certain classes of employment. That rate of remuneration is known and it is supposed to apply to all who are employed in a particular class. Had there been no strike, all who were engaged in performing a particular class of duties would have been receiving an amount 
of remuneration equivalent to that assignable to that particular class. There are some men who came iback into the postal service at Winnipeg under the terms of the order in council which permitted them to reenter. They were put into certain classes of work, but were put into these classes not at the rate of remuneration which these classes properly command but at a rate which was lower than that for which the service at which they were engaged should have been remunerated. This bill provides that where such was the case men shall be paid for the work they actually performed at the rates of pay attaching to the work of the class on which they were engaged. If, for example, a man was a letter carrier and was doing letter carrier's work, but was paid as a postal helper at a much lower rate, he would be entitled to the difference between the .postal helper's rate and the letter carrier's rate for the time during which he had been doing letter carrier's work; nothing, more. The same with respect to all other classes of employees. Now I ask hon. gentlemen:	Is not that obviously the fair
thing to do?
There is no necessity of confusing the present measure with any question that relates itself back to the reemployment of these men. If there was an error in their reemployment it is an error for which the present administration at all events is not responsible. We are not trying to saddle responsibility upon anyone with respect to the reemployment of these men. We say that the principle involved in their reemployment, whether right or wrong, was settled by the government in office in 1920. We are not even taking exception to the manner in which they settled the matter. But the fact is that they settled it without reference to any act or authority; they settled it in total disregard of the Civil Service Act. Hon. gentlemen have been saying a good deal about the attention that should be paid to the Civil Service Act. Well, the act was there, and if they had followed its provisions we should not now be discussing this matter. But they ignored the act altogether. My hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) thought they had proceeded under authority of the War Measures Act, but I find on going' into the matter that they ignored that act also. In other words, they followed no act; they proceeded without authority, and arbitrarily under order in council, to reemploy the men.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: I was careful to say that I did not know.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext:
Yes; my hon. friend did say that he did not know. But I wish to make it clear that, having 'looked into

Western Postal Employees-Mr. Mackenzie King
the matter, I find the facts as I state them. Be that as it may, however, we are all prepared,
I hope, to concede that at that particular time many things may have occurred which we tru3t will never occur again. But what we do say is that the question of reemployment, the right or the wrong of it, was settled at that time; and that, therefore, is not the principle which is to be settled at this moment.
Let us come now to what this particular measure seeks to do. It seeks to proceed in accordance with another principle, namely, that the state in hiring labour should pay for [DOT] services rendered in certain positions the rates of wages which those positions command, either in accordance with the current rate or in keeping with what may be fixed by the Civil Service Commission or by some other recognized authority. In all government employment there is a certain basis on which labour is paid, having regard to the amount and the quality of the work performed. In this particular matter there is no dispute regarding what certain classes of work of a particular quality command. It is known that a postal helper receives so much a day; that a sorter receives so much a day; that a letter carrier receives so much a day. And so on. Records are kept of the work of employees from day to day, and it is known whether men have worked as letter carriers or sorters or helpers. It is possible therefore to ascertain exactly the difference between what any man was paid and what he should have received had he not been penalized in the matter of his wages.
This bill seeks to remove, as respects actual service performed, a sense of injustice not only in the minds of the men immediately affected but in the minds of labour generally; because as the matter now stands the government of the country is in the position of seeking to depress standard rates of wages, and hon. gentlemen know that if labour is concerned about one thing above another it is the maintenance of certain standards in the matter of hours, wages and conditions of employment. We say there is no dispute as to the standard which should prevail with respect to wages, hours and conditions of employment in this particular post office at Winnipeg, and we believe that the state, as a model employer, should see to it that the men who have been reemployed and have done certain work should be given the full payment due them for the services they have performed. I trust that this explanation is clear. I do not think it leaves doubt in the mind of anyone, and I think this house would do itself a fuller measure of justice if it unanimously accepted the principle of the
payment of wages for actual work performed to those who have been so engaged especially where the men who have been reemployed have been reemployed by the state itself.

Will the Prime Minister
permit a question? In the light of the explanation he has just made, why has not the government for the last seven years paid employees wages for services rendered-a principle very clearly explained by the right hon. gentleman?

I hope the
government has done so. There may be some laws-the Civil Service Act for example- which operate in the matter. So far as I am concerned I stand strongly for the principle that employees, whether engaged by the government or by private industry, shall be paid for services actually rendered.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED
speechtext: The Prime Minister does not catch my question. I believe the
leader of the opposition said a moment ago that an effort was made last year and the year before, but apparently the excitement which the introduction of the measure provoked prevented our getting as far along with it as we have succeeded in doing this year with the present bill. The reason these men have been paid a lower rate for so many years is that the order in council which permitted their reemployment necessitated their reentering the service at a low rate. Had they been placed at and continued in the employment which commanded that low rate no exception could be taken at all to what was done. But what happened was this: The men who were qualified to act as sorters and letter carriers were obliged, under the order in council of reemployment, to enter as postal helpers and to receive the pay of postal helpers, although they were not given postal helpers' work to do. Many of them were put

But where a man entered at a postal helper's rate of pay and worked as a sorter or as a fetter carrier, we say that an injustice was done-an injustice which this bill seeks to remove.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF SALARIES OF THOSE DISMISSED AND REEMPLOYED

speakeroldname: Mr. L. S. R. MORIN (St. Hyacinthe-Rou-ville):
speechtext:
I desire to move in amendment to the motion for third reading:
That Bill No. 212, an act to amend the Customs Tariff, be not read a third time but be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions to amend item 460 F by adding thereto after the words "trough belt conveyors'' the words "of a class or kind not made in Canada."
My reason for proposing this amendment, Mr. Speaker, is that the belt manufacturers of Canada will be placed in a very difficult position if some action of this kind is not taken. In their competition with British and United States manufacturers they are handicapped by the fact that while their raw material is imported free they must pay on it higher transportation charges than they pay on the finished product, because the raw material is more bulky.
The raw material carries a lower freight rate.

But since it is more bulky the transportation charges are higher. Moreover, the manufacturers are handicapped by the action of this house in imposing a duty of fifty cents per ton on all their coal and a duty of 27i per cent on their machinery when it is of a kind made in Canada, or 10 per cent when it is of a kind not made in Canada. Under these circumstances the Canadian manufacturer is not in a position to meet the competition of the British manufacturer who is not affected by these duties, and as a matter of fact the Canadian industry is hardly able to meet the competition of the American industry even under a duty of 12^ per cent.
Let us suppose the American and the Canadian manufacturers were placed on the same footing; we could reasonably assume that they would divide the Canadian trade, and therefore 50 per cent of our consumption of this article would be furnished by American manufacturers to the detriment of Canadian labour. It seems to me that these are conditions which should not be approved by this house and which should not be the policy of the government; at a time when the balance of trade is so much in favour of the United States I think we should not continue to increase our purchases in that country and decrease the production in Canada, particularly when it is very clear that the Canadian consumer will not derive any benefit.
I think if we add to item 460 F a provision that the reduction in duty will apply only to trough belt conveyors not made in Canada the requirements of our industry will be satisfied and it will be for the general advantage of our country.
Might I ask whether the general effect would be an increase or a decrease in revenue?

It all depends on whether these articles are presently imported from the United States. If they are not imported now there is no revenue; if they
are imported of course it will increase the revenue.

I am very much surprised that any member of this house should once more seek to introduce into the tariff of Canada the most dangerous phrase ever invented. The clause says that articles shall come into Canada free which are "of a class and kind not manufactured in Canada." I have been endeavouring to ascertain from the ^Department of Finance who it was that invented this clause; I have been trying to ascertain when it was first introduced into a budget. It is an amazing thing to find this clause no less than nine times in the present budget. I object to the clause because it is a dangerous one. The province of Ontario has recently passed a bill permitting municipalities in that province-

Customs Tariff Amendment
What about the other provinces in Canada?

The province of Ontario
does not pass laws for any other province. This bill will permit municipalities to issue debentures to defray the cost of laying out sections of their cities or towns for industrial purposes. The city of Oshawa, where I come from, is a highly industralized community and we are asking authority to lay out a portion of the city for industrial purposes. What form of industry can we induce to come to the province of Ontario? Naturally we look into our imports to see just what articles are consumed in Canada, but when we look at the budget we find that articles which are not made in Canada are permitted to come in free. What encouragement is that for the industrial development of our province? The clause appears nine times in the present budget and I look upon it as a blight. I cannot imagine anything more injurious to the future of Canada than the continual injection of that clause into the industrial budgets of Canada, a clause which says that anything which is not made in Canada shall be allowed to come in free. The people of Canada want to manufacture as much as possible in Canada and not have it continually said that when an article is not made here it may come in free.

to these claims as he did, and said that out of loyalty to the administration he voted with them last year, although he felt they should pay the claims, he but presented the argument which we now make to this government, that having the money in hand which was paid by Germany for the purpose of reparations for the wrongs and injuries suffered by the civil population in the terms that were read this afternoon by the Secretary of State, then indeed we should proceed to discharge them. In other words, the money is there, the claims are now proven, judgment has been given by the commissioner, and on that judgment we should proceed to pay in full.
Let us proceed a step further. There was another reason. A very few claims had been considered by the late Mr. Pugsley. Some of the larger ones and the great multitude of the small claims which Mr. Commissioner Friel dealt with, had not, may I remind the hon. member for Cartier, even been considered by the commissioner. These claims that were referred to this afternoon, the claims that the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough mentioned, the claims in which we are all interested, are the claims of the small persons who have suffered by reason of not having received this money. I do say to the Minister of Finance, now that he has had the use of this money for all these years and 'has received $21,000,000 that enabled him to pay off obligations due by the Dominion, carrying interest at the rate of five per cent, he should with the remaining money and the accumulated benefits that have come to this treasury by the use of it all 'these years pay these claimants in full with interest at five per cent per annum in the terms of the judgment of Mr. Commissioner Friel. Why should this country retain the money which belongs to these people and not pay interest on it? Would a private individual do so? It is true there was no legal trust set up, but the very word " reparations " and the language that my hon. friend the Secretary of State this afternoon referred to, namely the injuries and the wrongs done to the civil population, indicate that this money-as indeed it was-was paid by Germany for one purpose, to discharge at least in part the damages that were done to the civil population by reason of the war. There seems to be no doubt about it on the part of all the members of this house. The hon. member for Cartier said three years ago the government recognized that principle; the opposition of that day said, you have not ample evidence before you to warrant you taking this step; the hon. member for 78594-166^
Vancouver Centre pointed out very distinctly aand clearly that fact; Sir Henry Drayton in his observations pointed out that it was late in the session and it should not be done. The right hon. leader of the opposition pointed out further that the money belonged to the state and they could do with it as they pleased. I say I am not discussing the legal rights; I never have. I have conceded always, so far as the state is concerned, that the obligation of parliament is not an obligation that can be measured in terms of exact contract. But the money was reparations money to repair the wrongs done to a civil population-not injuries suffered in the field, not defeats suffered on sea or land, but injuries done to the civil population through the war. The men who lost their fishing smacks, the men who loslt their nets, the men who lost their boats, the women whose husbands were loslt at sea-all these are losses of the civil population for which Germany, being responsible for the war, has paid a sum of money into the treasury of this country. These are losses which the civil population suffered and for which Germany, having been responsible for the war, has paid money into the treasury, and I think it ill becomes any Minister of Finance, whether it be the present incumbent of the office or some other, to state to this house that he will depart from the principle under which such moneys are paid. That principle is that such moneys shall be available to rectify the wrongs and injuries done the civil population of the country in consequence of the war. My hon. friend from Cartier and the Secretary of State take this attitude: they say that what this house thinks this house will do. That is a very fair attitude to take because, as has been pointed out, the wrongs were suffered not by one class of people alone; they were not suffered only by members who supported the administration, although one member is concerned in the net result. But not one member of parliament or two, not Liberals or Conservatives, are to be considered as such in dealing with the matter. That is not the point. Those who suffered these wrongs were citizens of Canada, and Germany has paid a sum of money to repair those wrongs, that sum of money being known as reparations.

The minister is only making matters worse. Apparently there were two occasions on which the government came to a decision that the money ought to be paid. The minister wasted a great deal of time this afternoon on the same subject. The , money is not yet paid over and nobody on this side of the chamber knows whether the government are going to pay in full now or not. Germany admitted .tih-at they were not able .to pay all the losses occasioned by the war, but they said they would pay the losses occasioned to thie civilian populations .of the countries involved, and they have already contributed a very large amount for that purpose. This government has received over $21,500,000 which they hold plus a good deal of .accumulated interest as from the date of the first payment, but nothing has been paid out yet. Hundreds of people in Nova Scotia and elsewhere in Canada have suffered and suffered severely for a long time. Some of the original sufferers are dead; many of them are in want. But the government insists, I think wrongfully, on withholding from those people money which should be paid to them on account of those losses. Germany paid that money on one account and one only; the government took that money from Germany, and if they do not pay it over to the people who sustained the losses, either they are guilty of taking money from Germany on false pretences or they are defrauding parties in this country who are entitled to those amountsone or the other. I have scant respect for the idea that this money belongs to the state, come from what source it may. If the government cannot deal justly with money that comes into their hands for a specific purpose, then woe betide the country.
As regards the question of interest, the government have held this money for years. They have either spent the interest or saved it; it is immaterial which. The people to whom the awards were made by the government's own commissioners after evidence taken and inquiries made, are entitled to the payment not only of the amount awarded by the commissioners appointed by the government, but to the interest. As to that there is no possible doubt. I am at a loss to understand why this or any other government should insist on keeping in the treasury money which does not belong to them, and which they received for a specific purpose and which is due people who are and have been in needy circumstances for many years.
I apprehend that probably the present intention of the minister although it has not yet 'been1 disclosed, is to now vote a portion of the amount. Certainly that was his intention when he brought down the resolution in the first place. I anticipate now, from the hedging which has been exhibited in the house this afternoon, that he intends later to bring down a bill providing for the payment of the balance. I suggest to him that it would be better for him, better for his government and better for the well-being and honour of the Dominion of Canada that he should pay the full amount this year, rather than next year immediately prior to a coming election. If he will take my advice in that matter, he will act accordingly. I only regret that I am not able to put this matter as effectively as I should like to. My leader has however, ably done so, and I again appeal to the government and to the minister to deal with this matter as they would deal with it if it were a matter in their own private business. We are sometimes told that members of the House of Commons coming here are sometimes not actuated by the best of motives. I repudiate that idea, which however the action of the government as outlined by the minister this afternoon goes far to give colour to. If the minister persists in the attitude which he has so far adopted a good many people in this country will have occasion to blaspheme.

I would ask the hon. Secretary of State to take into consideration the real mind of this parliament, and I suggest that because he has shown himself dis-

posed not to put a limit upon the amount but rather to offer opportunity to increase it. I am familiar myself with many cases of hardship, and I think that nothing else will do but paying the full amount of these claims according to the judgments that 'have been given. The people of Canada will not be satisfied with less. You cannot pay just a certain percentage, 20 per cent or 50 per cent; you cannot single out some and deny others; you cannot make a choice between those who can afford to do without the awards and those who cannot. In a matter of this kind the full amount of the claim has to be reckoned. As the hon. gentleman who preceded me said, in 1919 the attitude then taken was to recognize these claims and to pay them. The Secretary of State says that it is an ex gratia payment. So it is in law.. None of these private individuals would have a lawsuit against Germany; that is well understood, but that money has been paid in respect of a specific application, and I say it would be fraud on the part of this country if these claims were not recognized.
An automobile accident takes place. The father is in the car with his child. Both are injured. The father is awarded so much for himself and so much for his child. The child cannot take the money but his claim is paid; it is an ex gratia payment if you like, but who would say that the father could appropriate that money to himself? He is not allowed to touch a cent of it. So I say when this money has been given to Canada for a specific purpose, why should the Dominion of Canada say how that money should be spent? Why" apply it to the consolidated revenue fund? Why should the government say: We are going to make a payment for which we should be complimented, if we recompense in part those who have suffered? Let me tell the Secretary of State that the people of Canada will never be satisfied unless the specific money has the specific application which it was intended to have, and I am satisfied that the people of this country will say that those who have suffered damages should be recompensed according to the judgments handed down.

Secretary of State that something further should be done before the matter is finally disposed of. I am sure that we are

I believe that in doing so he is acting wisely. I feel sure that unless this matter is dealt with in a way that will appeal to the claimants and also be approved by the people of the country generally, it will not be settled satisfactorily.
The bill provides for the settlement of some fourteen hundred1 claims. There are only a few others, no doubt large ones, but I think possibly the government would be well advised to endeavour to take care of them also.
My main object in rising at this stage is to advocate the payment of interest in connection with these claims. There are different reasons, and I think good reasons, that can be advanced in favour of that course. One is that the government has had this money for some time, and as has already been stated, the money has been earning interest for the government, so the government would not be much out of pocket if they paid the interest on these claims. Another reason, and I think it is perhaps a stronger one, is this: We are now acknowledging these claims. If we acknowledge these claims _I contend that we are admitting the principle that that money has been held by the government in trust for the different claimants, and if the money has been so held by the government, it is in duty bound to pay interest on the claims.
The question next arises as to the date from which interest should begin. That is a very material matter to the claimants, because if you -will read over the different claims you will find that a great many different dates have been stated. I have in mind two claims one of which I am interested in. Both these parties lost properties on the same date in 1918. The claims were adjusted) by the same man, but he recommended that interest be paid in the one case from 1918, and in the other only from 1923. That is a matter that will have to be looked into very carefully before the money is paid over. I observe that the United States has admitted the payment of interest on all claims from the one date, from September 16, 1928. I do not know whether the claimants in Canada would be satisfied with a settlement of that kind-
I do not think they would; but I think possibly the government could arrive at a decision to pay interest on all the claims from a certain date. That is a position which the government could very well take, and it is one to which not much objection could be

taken. We should approach this matter not in any spirit of party recrimination or faultfinding. The minister has shown his willingness to meet the views of the house, and I think we can trust him to da so. I am highly pleased with the attitude he has taken to-night. I feel that nothing that the government has done this session will be received in the country with more enthusiasm and more appreciation than its settlement of these claims. We have settled other claims in this parliament. We settled the claim of the automobile dealers who were asking for a refund some years ago; the Home bank depositors had their claims dealt with, and only to-day we passed a bill providing compensation for the postal workers in western Canada. I think therefore that the house would be well advised to go as far as we possibly can in adjusting these claims and making a clean job of the matter. Let us provide the money and the interest, and let the interest be fixed to run from a certain date, and then I think that the people will thank the government and the members who advocated this measure.
