speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I desire to direct my remarks to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. King) with regard to this vote. The minister, of course, is perfectly well aware that the Department of Health was created in 1919 for several specific purposes, the more important of which have not been carried out by the department. The main activities of the department since that date have been generally in connection with various kinds of work which were formerly done by other departments. Those works were of importance in themselves, but they were very efficiently administered by other departments before the health department was brought into existence at all. In themselves they did not constitute a real cause for the organization of a department of health, and as a matter of fact they were not considered a reason for the creation of that department, but were simply thrown in, I might say, as ballast.
The conditions existing after the war had something to do with the creation of a health department. The control of venereal disease, the coordination of health activities of the provinces into a unit, and the establishment of a bureau of scientific research with regard to health, were the real basic reasons for the creation of a health department. Since that time it has not in any way attempted to implement the basic purposes for which it was created in 1919. So far as the control of venereal disease is concerned the department apparently thought they had done their duty when they relegated the matter to the provincial departments of health and gave them
8100,000	a year to be distributed pro rata to population. Not even on the question of immigration, where large numbers of people were coming into this country, did the depart-
2618	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
ment attempt to control this disease or to find out those suffering from it, although the department must have known quite well that in the free clinics of our various hospitals 60 per cent of those asking for free treatment for the disease were members of our foreign population. Scarcely anything was done to keep out that class of people; the only class they attempted to exclude were those suffering from syphilis.	*
Inso far as coordination of the various health activities of the provinces is concerned, nothing was done but to appoint a Dominion council of health. That council was constituted of men eminent in the medical profession and in other walks of life, representing the departments of health in the various provinces and certain departments of the government as well as outside societies. I think the council was constituted of about fifteen members, but they were practically crippled in their efforts to do anything in relation to public health. They were earnest and desirous of doing something for the public health of Canada, but they were not given any facilities or any means by which they could carry any project to a successful conclusion. Consequently they confined their efforts to giving advice.
So far as the real basic reason for establishing the health department is concerned, that is, the bringing about of a bureau of scientific research, not even has it been spoken of so far as I know by any official of the department or by any member of the government. Since the day of the organization of the department nothing has been done in any way to establish a bureau of scientific research. I know the government has a laboratory of hygiene upon which a few thousands each year have been spent, but that has nothing whatever to do with scientific research. I do not wish to minimize the benefit of even the laboratory of hygiene, I think it has done fairly good work in looking after the purity of food, standardizing drugs, and also in analyzing patent and proprietary medicine. It has done some work of that kind-; but with regard to the establishment o-f scientific research nothing has been done at all. I do not need to t-el'l the minister, because he knows it himself, that the establishment of a real research institute properly equipped and manned would be one bf the best agencies for the promotion of good health in Canada that could be -had. He knows that it would be a centre around which the activities of the various provinces would revolve, and it would create in Ottawa a health department which would- be an asset to the country instead of a

liability. It would be a sort of clearing house for health information and would help to -coordinate the activities of the various health departments in the provinces which are now doing good work. I am of the opinion that the establishment of a scientific research bureau is the one thing needed to coordinate the efforts of t-he various health departments of the nation into a unit Which would perform a splendid service in the Dominion. There are many and substantial reasons why the government should take this matter into serious consideration at the earliest opportunity in the future and establish a bureau of scientific research.
The greatest asset of a country is its people, *and the greatest asset of a people is good health. There is no doubt on that score. Good health gives a vigorous body, a sound mind and great mental activity, with initiative, resourcefulness and ability an-d courage to carry projects into effect. These attributes of body and mind are influenced by many factors, some of them natural and o-thers under our control. Professor Fisher of Yale, making a demand for a scientific health institute in the United States, made the statement that the future belongs to the nation that has the greatest inventive genius. I think that is correct, but I -would go further and say that, other things being equal, the future belongs to the nation that keeps the health of its people up to the highest standard. Mr. Hoover, making a speech in the city of New York only a short time ago, said that we were entering a period of increased competition from the reconstructed nations of Europe. That is quite correct; everyone will agree with it; and I might go further and say that increased -population and the increased propagation of scientific knowledge and methods will increase competition still further, so that only those nations that are alive to the necessity of a vigorous citizenship will be able to take leadership or maintain it. Canada should have little difficulty in doing this because nature has endowed us with two of the main contributing factors. Nature has given us a splendid climate in a north temperate zone, a climate which is conducive to strong, vigorous and mentally active people. We have the nucleus of that people now, and Professor McLennan of Toronto university, when he appeared before the special committee on industrial research, made this statement with regard to our people:
Canadians have an intellect, a freshness of mind, a virility, a broad outlook and a resourcefulness not excelled in .any country in the world.

Supply[DOT]-Pensions and National Health
I think most hon. members in this house will agree with that statement. Again, we have a country teeming with natural resources of such a wide variety that we have the raw material for almost every kind of industry; and having the people there is no reason in the world why we should not forge ahead with great strides towards leadership amongst the nations. But, Mr. Chairman, great natural resources are of little use if the people have not the intelligence and energy enough to make use of them. Large areas of agricultural land are useful and valuable just in proportion to the quality and the extent of cultivation. Great mineral resources are valueless if they are left buried in the ground. It needs a healthy, energetic people to turn these resources into wealth. I say, therefore, that we in Canada are neglecting the greatest asset this country has. Are we going to continue in our present haphazard methods with regard to these conditions that exist to-day? We should give direction from the city of Ottawa to the health activities of the whole Dominion. The one thing needed to weld these various activities into an efficient whole that would give proper service is a bureau of scientific research in health, a bureau which would bring the brightest scientific minds in the medical profession into this city, giving them the facilities which would enable them to undertake research in the cure and prevention of disease. I do not think anyone in this chamber could estimate the value to the Dominion of Canada of a cure and preventive for the flu, or influenza, or even a common cold. It would be impossible to estimate the benefits that would accrue to mankind; you could not compute it in dollars and cents. It is beyond human computation. Yet that is something that will be found in the future, and it should be our duty at least to make an attempt in this Dominion to solve that problem. It is estimated that the deaths from flu in 1918 were many times greater than the number of deaths caused by the Great war. Senator Copeland, at one time Minister of Health in New York, said that the deaths caused by influenza in 1918 exceeded the deaths caused by all the wars of history. I should not care bo go to that extent, but I am satisfied that the number was very large indeed. Professor Fisher of Yale university made an estimate of the economic loss to the United States in a single year from loss in wages due to preventable illness and premature deaths, and he placed that loss at fifteen billions of dollars. If that estimate is right as regards the United States, then the loss in Canada annually from the same cause amounts to between a billion and a billion and a half. Surely it is
worth while on behalf of the people of this country for us to take such steps as we may to prevent such losses year by year.
The Great war stimulated medical and scientific research. It has been well said that necessity is the mother of invention, and the unusual difficulties with which the medical forces of the world armies were faced during the war stimulated them to find remedies to meet the various cases with which they had to deal. In all the previous wars of history disease carried off many times more soldiers than were killed by the enemy, but the Great war was a signal vindication of medical science. The war could not have been carried on but for the advances which have been made in medical and sanitary science during the last twenty-five years. Disease and pestilence would have decimated the armies if they had not been able to avail themselves of these discoveries.
Typhoid fever always has been the great scourge of war. During the South African war, in which only 200,000 men were engaged; 80 men died from typhoid to every 20 men who died from their wounds. There were over
60,000	cases of typhoid fever, with 8,227 deaths. During the Great war ten times that number of men were engaged in the British army; they were engaged in the field for four and a half years, yet during that time there were only 4,571 cases of typhoid fever with a mortality of 1.3 peT cent. Through the advance of medical science the ratio of deaths from disease and deaths due to enemy bullets was reversed; 20 men died from disease to SO men who died from wounds, and one writer has gone so far as to say that 95 per cent of the deaths in the Great war resulted from wounds and only 5 per cent from disease. The victory over typhoid fever was the greatest success of the war, and it was brought about by the use of a preventive serum and by sanitation, as far as that .could be carried out.
Another great success of the war was the victory over tetanus. The medical corps of the different armies were very much exercised over the dangers which might exist in the highly cultivated soil of Flanders and France, which contained a large amount of fertilizer; it was realized that the soil would be teeming with the bacillus of tetanus. A serum had been developed previous to the war but had not been thoroughly tested; it was brought into use, and the results were wonderful. Tetanus was practically eliminated as a cause of death during the Great war.
Malaria has been stated by one writer to have been the cause of the fall of Rome and
2620	COMMONS
Supply-Pensions and National Health
the decadence of Greece. Malaria took a hand in the Great war; on the Macedonian and Mesopotamian fronts malaria was a more formidable enemy than the Bulgarian or Turkish troops. The mortality from that cause was very high; many men were invalided home and it cost the British government millions of pounds in after years to bring these men back to any degree of health, and many of them are still suffering from a recurrence of the disease. The campaign on the Gallipoli front was a failure because of malaria and dysentery among the troops, dvsentery both of the amoebic and bacillary varieties. There was no real remedy at that time for these two diseases, which were mainly caused by the large number of flies in that hot climate, but before the campaign ended the medical service perfected two remedies which were very effective indeed, and from that time on the deaths were very few in comparison to what they had been previously.
A federal health institute of research has been provided for in the act which was passed in 1919, and all that is required is an amount of money placed in the estimates sufficient to care for the organization of that department. Subsection (a) of section 4 of chapter 24 provides for cooperation with the various health departments of the provinces, while subsection (b) provides for the establishment of a bureau of scientific research. In moving the second reading of the bill Mr. Rowell is reported at page 1171 of Hansard for 1919 as follows:
-I should think that one of the natural and inevitable developments of a federfal department of health would be a bureau of scientific research in connection with it.
The power is there and, as I have said, the only thing lacking is an amount in the estimates sufficient to provide for the organization of this department. Professor Fisher of Yale, in advocating a health institute in the United States, said:
The heads of all the leading research bodies and medical organizations testify that the proposed national institute of health will not duplicate their work, but will rather help to focus it better.
I am of opinion that a scientific institute here in Ottawa would focus the health activities of the Dominion and make them very much more effective. Such an institution would be a clearing house for the provinces, particularly with relation to epidemic diseases. At present there is no method by which the various activities of the provinces can be brought together and the information developed in one province communicated to 
the others. A scientfic research bureau here would accomplish that purpose.
In 1917, when the Military Service Act was enforced, a little over 50 per cent of the men examined were rejected because of disease; of 361,655 men examined 181,225 were rejected. Of those rejected almost 60 per cent were found physically unfit because of preventable diseases. Surely it is a severe indictment of the public health activities of the Dominion of Canada when so many men were found physical^ unfit because of diseases they should not have had.
A great deal of research work has been done, much of it by private individuals and by our universities in a rather desultory way; many men work by themselves, yet even so a great many discoveries of immense benefit to the world have been made. What is the value of those great discoveries of the past to the people of the world? Jenner discovered a vaccine for smallpox. Can anyone estimate the value of that one discovery? It goes on in increasing volume as the years go by and it will continue throughout the centuries. When a remedy is discovered for a disease the value continues for ever. Pasteur discovered a remedy for hydrophobia. Lister discovered antiseptics which revolutionzed surgery and made it possible to perform surgical operations which otherwise would have proved fatal. Cavities of the body may be invaded and diseased tissue removed with impunity because of that discovery. What is the value to be put upon the discoveries of Simpson and Morton in the matter of anaesthetics? Surgery was revolutionized when the. groaning and struggling patient was made to lie quiet while the operation was performed without pain. Banting through his discovery of insulin has done a great deal for people suffering from diabetes. He has lengthened their lives and made them happier. Reed and Carroll discovered the cause of yellow fever and made it possible to complete the Panama canal. Klebs and Loeffler discovered the bacillus of diphtheria and made the first step in the direction of producing a serum which has practically eliminated that loathsome disease which is very fatal to children. Are these discoveries worth anything to the world? No one can estimate their value, and if anyone doubts their value he has only to get one of the diseases and he will realize what it means to him.
There are still many worlds to conquer in the realm of medicine and we should do our share in that regard, and at the same time consolidate our position with regard to the discoveries which have been made in the

Supply-Pensions and National Health
past. At times such discoveries are not used because of the indifference of public health authorities and the ignorance of the people. I was interested in reading the other day an article by Doctor Rajchman, director of health organizations of the League of Nations, in which he drew attention to the fact that smallpox had not yet been eliminated from the world although we had a very effective remedy in the vaccine discovered by Jenner. Many people have a feeling that the vaccine caused other diseases. He gave a list of the epidemics which have occurred in the last few years, as follows:
Minneapolis	 1925
Detroit	 1924
Los Angeles	 1927
Algeria	 1927
Rio de Janiero	 1926
He reported that in 1927 there were 280,000 certified cases of smallpox reported in the world, and during that same year 50,000 deaths occurred in India from the same disease. He also reported that the death rates in these epidemics ranged from 10 to 30 per cent. In 1927 there was an epidemic of smallpox in Indiana, which has no compulsory vaccination law. In 1885 there was an epidemic of smallpox in Montreal and Quebec, and 7,000 deaths. In 1884, the previous year, the Ontario Medical Health Act was passed. As soon as the outbreak occurred in Quebec the Ontario health authorities organized 563 local boards of health and appointed 283 medical officers and 160 sanitary inspectors. They enforced compulsory vaccination and the result was that the epidemic was stopped in that province with a loss of only 18 lives. That illustrates what can be done when science is fully organized.
In 1928 the city of Olean, New York, had an epidemic of typhoid fever caused by infected water. Actions were brought against the health department and judgments were granted to the amount of $350,000. Application was made to the state legislature for an enabling act to allow them to issue bonds to pay these damages, and they will be paying for the neglect of their health department for the next twenty years. The city of Albany, New York, has also had judgments rendered against it for the same cause, and I should think the city of Ottawa would take warning. No city I have ever visited had so vile a water supply as this city.
What is being done outside of looking after the human element in the Dominion of Canada? When I consider the estimates for other departments I find that more is being done for them than is being done for the public health of the country. In 1916 the national research council was set up to promote the utilization of our natural resources and to find means of using the waste products from the same, as well as to carry on other duties. This council is composed of some of the most prominent scientists of Canada. The council has given 344 scholarships to 199 persons who have shown special adaptability for scientific research. Young men are being turned out in our universities trained in medical and other sciences, but year after year they go to the United States and the universities of that country are filled with Canadians who have been trained here. They have been forced to take that step because we do not employ them.
We spend millions on agriculture and we have brought it to a very high state of efficiency. The 1930 estimates for this department amount to $8,483,000. Of that amount $2,450,000 is being asked for the health of animals branch, and $1,530,000 for the improvement of live stock. That amount spent upon the public health of Canada would be very acceptable, and would make a very splendid contribution to scientific research.
The estimates of this year include an item of $730,540 for the mines and geological survey. Of that amount $257,000 is for the investigation of mineral resources and deposits, and $363,000 for the geological survey.
We are spending $2,403,000 in an endeavour to make the fishing industry of this country profitable. Of that amount $442,000 is for the culture of fish, $301,000 for scientific and practical work, making a total of $743,000 spent in scientific work for the benefit of the fisheries of this country.

some of it, I am sure, is spent in connection with quarantine stations for other purposes. That makes a total of $490,000 for the health of human beings in Canada. It is surely a reflection on the intelligence of the Dominion parliament that such a situation exists to-day Millions for the health of animals, millions for bringing immigrants into Canada, and millions for mining and fishing, but a paltry five hundred thousand dollars to improve the condition of health of the people.
I do not intend to labour this question much further, but I should like to read what President Hoover has to say with regard to the situation in the United States and his desire for further organization of the health department. In his speech made on March 1 of this year Mr. Hoover says this:
Public health service should be as fully organized and as universally incorporated into our governmental system as our public education system to-day. The returns are a thousandfold in economic benefits and infinitely more in reduction of suffering and promotion of human happiness.
I direct the attention of the Minister of National Health to these statements and I would say that if next year he will decide to insert in the estimates an amount that will provide a building, equip and man it for the purpose of scientific research in health, the money will be returned to him, not a thousandfold, but many thousandfold, and if in future years they are able to find a remedy and preventive for the flu, the amount spent will return to him so many times over that he will be surprised. I therefore ask the minister to take this matter into his serious consideration and turn the present Health department of the Dominion of Canada, which is now doing some work but which is inefficient and not carrying out the provisions of the Health Act as it was intended by the government and parliament which passed it in 1919, into a real asset to the country so that it will be worthy of his tenure of office.

May I supplement what the last speaker has said in his very excellent address by a few statements which I should like to place on the record as appearing in a pamphlet issued by the Canadian Social Hygiene Council, as follows:
Figures would appear to prove that from 45 to 60 per cent of all disabling illness is of external origin and, therefore, within the possibility of prevention.
Various authentic estimates would show that 2 to 3 per cent of the total population is continuously ill.
Of the population of Canada, 30 per cent are adult males; 30 per cent are adult females.
It is thus estimated that 54,000 adult males are continuously ill. This amount of illness

would suggest that in the adult male population alone there are lost each year 16,200,000 working days.
Calculations show that, for every 20 males gainfully employed, there are aproximately G females similarly employed. This would suggest that, in addition, the female population loses
4,800,000	working days per year.
Total loss per year-21,000,000 working days; at least 50 per cent preventable.
Superfluous loss per year 10,500,000 working days.
It is important to bear in mind that the resultant cost must be reckoned not only in terms of loss of pay to employees, but also in terms of diminished output, disorganization of industry and other economic results.
It is estimated that the total cost of illness to the Dominion of Canada per year is $270,000,000, which equals 75 per cent of the total expenditure of the Dominion Government for 1924.
This pamphlet is several years old. There has been little opportunity for discussing this matter and now I do not want to say very much with regard to it. It is most unfortunate that there is no provision in this house for the careful study of an important ques-of this kind. I would venture to suggest that we could not do (better than set uip a committee on public health that would definitely devote itself to a study of the whole field of public health. Here we come to a Friday evening at nearly 11 o'clock, and this is about the only opportunity we have in the course of the whole session for a discussion of a question of this kind.

I know the minister docs not expect to get much through to-night, but I think it is his duty to give the committee a resume of the doings in his department. I

Supply-Pensions and National Health
have been in the house for a good many years. I was one who helped to bring the Health Act into existence. With one exception I have never known anything to happen but what has happened to-night; at eleven o'clock on Friday night the estimates of this department have always been brought in. I think this is a reflection upon the intelligence of the house, upon the people of Canada and upon the minister and the government who have for ten years sat in office and have had at their disposal a department which should be a most useful one in this or any other government. I say without contradiction that it has failed in every particular for which it was brought into existence. The minister smiles. On Monday probably I will give him some facts that may change that smile. I remember quite well, when this act was brought down in the old museum, the late Mr. Carvell coming to me afterwards and saying: "MeGibbon, you are only making positions for a lot more employees; you are only going to add to the country's expense; you will accomplish nothing." I was shocked that a minister of the crown should make such a statement upon such a subject. I have said before that I was speaking as a prophet, and to-night the voice of history records the accuracy of my prophecy as to the accomplishments of this department, which have been nothing up to the present time. It has been nothing but a bill of expense to the country, and it has failed in every particular to do what it was intended it should do. I intend to have something more to say on this subject on Monday. As it is now five minutes to eleven, I do not suppose the minister expects to get any estimates through to-night, and I think he should come to this house on Monday or whenever the estimates come up again prepared to give parliament and the country some account of his stewardship during the last five or six years. The report which has been handed out by the department is nothing but a catalogue.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Under this vote we provide for the care and maintenance in outside institutions and in mental institutions of the men who served overseas and who suffered disabilities; also for drugs, medical and surgical supplies, and dental treatment and supplies, medical examination and observation of pensioners, manufacture and purchase of orthopedic, ophthalmic and surgical appliances, supplies and repairs, and for the transportation of patients and pensioners.
Under the heading of departmental institutions the expenditure was $797,004.38; in outside hospitals and for doctors, $1,252,661.93; indirect charges, transportation of patients, escorts $50,085.61; funeral expenses $25,673.24; expenses of travelling medical boards $5,062.27; transportation of pensioners $47,576.24, or a total of $128,397.96. The expenditure for limb 
factory operations was $263,204.22. Altogether the total expenditure was $2,441,268.49.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
As the item is
worded it consists of two parts, pensions and health. We are now dealing with the first part, pensions, and in order to save time I would ask the minister to come prepared on Monday or when next his estimates are up to give an account of what has been done by way of reorganization in that department : second, the amount apportioned under this heading to each province. It would save time if the minister would also give the same information with regard to pensions. Third, as to sheltered employment, and fourth, as to the officers who have been retired within the last two years and those who have been added to the staff by provinces, together with the allowances to those who retired.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH

I shall be glad

Progress reported.
